text: RH4).4,17-20 In children and patients whose clinical or bacteriological response is slow, treat- ment should be extended to a total of 9 months.18-20 Chil- dren with extrapulmonary tuberculosis involving the bones or CNS, or in those with miliary disease, should be given treatment for a minimum of 12 months.18 Treatment failures in HIV-infected patients have been associated with reduced drug concentrations due to malabsorption of an- timycobacterials.21 Most clinicians would defer starting antiretroviral therapy in HIV co-infected patients with CD4+ counts greater than 200/microlitre until the tuberculosis treatment has been completed. Patients with more severe immunodeficiency benefit from co-administration of HIV and tuberculosis therapy. In these patients, tuberculosis therapy is started first, and HIV treatment added once the patient tolerates tuberculosis therapy, or after 2 months when tuberculosis therapy is simplified. The use of rifamycin-based regi- mens to treat tuberculosis is recommended as response rates are better compared to non-rifamycin-based regi- mens. However, drug interactions between rifamycins and antiretrovirals complicate the co-administration of HIV and tuberculosis treatment,19,20,22 and certain combina- tions may require dose adjustment or be contra-indicated (for details of the interactions of rifampicin and antiretro- virals see p.327 and for those with rifabutin see p.324). It is important to note that guideline recommendations are based on pharmacokinetic studies, often performed in healthy subjects, rather than on studies of treatment out- come in patients. Directly observed therapy improves outcome and is rec- ommended wherever possible. Due to the risk for acquired rifamycin resistance highly intermittent (once or twice weekly) tuberculosis regimens should not be used for co- infected patients with CD4+ cell counts less than 100 cells/microlitre.18-20,22 All HIV and tuberculosis co- infected patients should receive co-trimoxazole if CD4+ counts are below 200 cells/microlitre.23 Thioacetazone should not be used in HIV-positive patients because of the potential for severe skin toxicity. Paradoxical worsening of tuberculosis symptoms is common in HIV-infected pa- tients who start antiretroviral therapy24 and incidences of up to 35% have been noted.22 • Adjunctive therapy. The inflammatory response to tu- berculosis can cause considerable tissue damage and ad- junctive steroid therapy may be used to counter this. Cor- ticosteroids are of little benefit in uncomplicated pulmonary tuberculosis. However, a study25 found adjunc- tive dexamethasone improved survival, but probably not severe disability, in adolescents and adults with tubercu- lous meningitis.
